questions.stem: An NP7 cluster changes roles quickly, but GARP appears late. Which setting directly changes hardware link-detection cadence?

choices.text: np-link-scan-interval controls NP7 link-state scan cadence.
choices.feedback: This is the dedicated NP7 link-scan control; it can shorten detection before FGCP processes the event.

choices.text: hb-interval controls FGCP peer heartbeat transmission.
choices.feedback: Heartbeat cadence is separate from the NP7 physical-link scan interval.

choices.text: failover-threshold controls missed heartbeat count before failover.
choices.feedback: The threshold changes heartbeat-based failure detection, not NP7 link polling.

choices.text: session-pickup controls session synchronization between cluster members.
choices.feedback: Session pickup affects session continuity, not when hardware detects link-down.

questions.stem: What interval does Fortinet document for NP7 link scanning?

choices.text: Default 500 ms, supported range 100–2000 ms.
choices.feedback: Those values do not match the documented default or range.

choices.text: Default 1000 ms, supported range 50–1000 ms.
choices.feedback: The dedicated NP7 guide documents 1000 ms by default and a 50–1000 ms range.

choices.text: Default 100 ms, supported range 10–500 ms.
choices.feedback: The lower bound is below the documented range and the default is wrong.

choices.text: Default 2000 ms, supported range 500–5000 ms.
choices.feedback: The proposed default and maximum exceed the documented interval.

questions.stem: Which part of the failover chain does a lower NP7 interval not change?

choices.text: Time until the NP7 hardware notices a physical link failure.
choices.feedback: This is the direct behavior the setting changes.

choices.text: Delay before the first GARP is emitted after role activation.
choices.feedback: Earlier detection can move the start of the GARP stage sooner.

choices.text: FGCP heartbeat, election, session pickup, and routing convergence.
choices.feedback: The interval only affects hardware link detection; it does not tune the other HA or routing stages.

choices.text: The scan cadence for NP7 physical interface link state.
choices.feedback: This is exactly the hardware scan cadence controlled by the setting.

questions.stem: Which evidence best proves that the new primary actually transmitted GARP?

choices.text: A cluster status page showing the new primary role.
choices.feedback: Role status does not show the GARP packet itself.

choices.text: A configuration dump showing the selected NP7 scan interval.
choices.feedback: Configuration proves the value, not the emitted packet.

choices.text: An HA event log showing the monitored interface went down.
choices.feedback: The event log proves detection, not neighbor notification.

choices.text: A SPAN capture showing GARP sourced by the new primary.
choices.feedback: A packet capture directly proves the GARP frame was transmitted on the observed segment.

questions.stem: The HA role transition itself is slow, before GARP is emitted. What should be examined first?

choices.text: Heartbeat reachability, monitored interfaces, and cluster election health.
choices.feedback: Those controls govern FGCP detection and election, which occur before GARP.

choices.text: Upstream ARP cache age and switch MAC-table aging.
choices.feedback: These affect neighbor convergence after failover, not the slow role transition.

choices.text: The client certificate OCSP responder and RADIUS policy.
choices.feedback: OCSP is unrelated to HA role selection.

choices.text: FortiAnalyzer Asset List and EMS connector freshness.
choices.feedback: Asset enrichment does not participate in FortiGate HA.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes FortiManager Manual and VRRP HA modes?

choices.text: Manual moves a VIP automatically; VRRP requires an operator promotion.
choices.feedback: The behaviors are reversed.

choices.text: Both modes always use the same shared VIP and election process.
choices.feedback: Manual mode does not use the same VRRP VIP mechanism.

choices.text: Manual requires operator promotion; VRRP can move a shared VIP automatically.
choices.feedback: Manual promotion is operator-driven; VRRP uses a monitored interface and virtual address.

choices.text: VRRP synchronizes policies, while Manual synchronizes only device inventory.
choices.feedback: Both modes replicate module data; this is not their defining distinction.

questions.stem: What is the documented default heartbeat detection window in FortiManager 7.6.6?

choices.text: 1-second heartbeat interval multiplied by 10 missed heartbeats.
choices.feedback: These values produce a much shorter and undocumented detection window.

choices.text: 10-second heartbeat interval multiplied by 30 missed heartbeats.
choices.feedback: The documented defaults produce 300 seconds, or five minutes, before the threshold is reached.

choices.text: 5-second heartbeat interval multiplied by 5 missed heartbeats.
choices.feedback: Those values do not match the documented defaults.

choices.text: 30-second heartbeat interval multiplied by 10 missed heartbeats.
choices.feedback: The interval and threshold are both mis-stated.

questions.stem: What is the default FortiManager HA file quota and its documented range?

choices.text: 2048 MB default, configurable from 1024 to 8192 MB.
choices.feedback: The default and range are lower than documented.

choices.text: 8192 MB default, configurable from 4096 to 32768 MB.
choices.feedback: The default is twice the documented default and the maximum is too high.

choices.text: 1024 MB default, configurable from 512 to 4096 MB.
choices.feedback: The documented minimum is 2048 MB, not 512 MB.

choices.text: 4096 MB default, configurable from 2048 to 20480 MB.
choices.feedback: The HA guide documents 4096 MB by default and a 2048–20480 MB range.

questions.stem: What does Pending Module Data indicate in FortiManager HA?

choices.text: Managed FortiGate devices that are currently unreachable by management traffic.
choices.feedback: Device reachability is a different management-plane state.

choices.text: Replication data still waiting to synchronize to the backup unit.
choices.feedback: Pending Module Data measures synchronization backlog between HA members.

choices.text: The number of policy packages awaiting administrator approval.
choices.feedback: Policy approvals are not what this HA counter measures.

choices.text: The count of missed heartbeat packets since the last role change.
choices.feedback: Heartbeat loss is tracked separately from module data replication.

questions.stem: What can happen when the FortiManager delta-sync file quota is exhausted?

choices.text: The queue can reset and synchronization can restart from a fresh state.
choices.feedback: The documented quota failure can reset the delta queue and restart synchronization.

choices.text: The secondary automatically becomes primary and moves the VIP.
choices.feedback: Quota exhaustion is not itself a VRRP or role-election event.

choices.text: All managed FortiGates are removed from the device database.
choices.feedback: The device database is not deleted by the queue reset.

choices.text: The primary stops sending heartbeat packets until quota is increased.
choices.feedback: Heartbeat and delta-sync storage are separate mechanisms.

questions.stem: An asset appears with MAC and IP but no hostname, OS, or user details. What is the likely explanation?

choices.text: The Industrial Security Service license has expired for every asset.
choices.feedback: The OT/IoT license controls vulnerability details, not basic hostname enrichment for all assets.

choices.text: The Asset Identity Center is configured to suppress all user identities.
choices.feedback: The missing fields are not explained by a global suppression setting.

choices.text: The vulnerability playbook has changed the endpoint MAC address.
choices.feedback: The playbook does not rewrite endpoint MAC addresses.

choices.text: The endpoint was discovered from logs without managed FortiClient EMS enrichment.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents limited identity fields when endpoints are detected without FortiClient context.

questions.stem: Which action retrieves managed-endpoint vulnerability data for the Asset List?

choices.text: Get Endpoints through the FortiGate traffic-log connector only.
choices.feedback: Get Endpoints retrieves endpoint details, not the vulnerability list by itself.

choices.text: Run a FortiSwitch MAC poll against every access port.
choices.feedback: A switch MAC poll does not retrieve endpoint vulnerability data.

choices.text: Get Vulnerabilities through the FortiClient EMS connector.
choices.feedback: The documented enrichment path uses Get Vulnerabilities with an EMS connector.

choices.text: Export the Top 10 Risky Assets widget to CSV.
choices.feedback: Exporting a widget does not trigger source enrichment.

questions.stem: What is required to view OT/IoT vulnerability details in the Asset List?

choices.text: A FortiClient EMS license assigned to every unmanaged sensor.
choices.feedback: EMS enriches managed endpoints; it does not replace the OT/IoT service license.

choices.text: A vSphere connector configured for all OT network segments.
choices.feedback: The vSphere connector is for VMware endpoint details, not OT vulnerability licensing.

choices.text: A valid Industrial Security Service license for the OT/IoT vulnerability feed.
choices.feedback: Fortinet states that OT/IoT vulnerability details require Industrial Security Service entitlement.

choices.text: A daily log-forwarding policy from FortiAnalyzer to FortiGate.
choices.feedback: Log forwarding is not the required entitlement.

questions.stem: Why might an asset be absent from Top 10 Vulnerable Assets despite having findings?

choices.text: The widget includes only endpoints discovered by MAC address.
choices.feedback: MAC-only discovery is not the stated widget exclusion rule.

choices.text: The widget excludes low-severity vulnerabilities; inspect the detailed table.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that low-severity vulnerabilities are omitted from that Top 10 widget.

choices.text: The widget excludes all findings older than one hour.
choices.feedback: The time filter can matter, but the documented severity exclusion is the key distinction.

choices.text: The widget displays only assets with a FortiGate serial number.
choices.feedback: A FortiGate serial number is not a required asset identity.

questions.stem: What is the key behavior of a PTP transparent clock?

choices.text: It updates the Sync correctionField for time spent inside the switch.
choices.feedback: A transparent clock corrects for residence time and does not participate in BMCA.

choices.text: It becomes grandmaster whenever the upstream Announce message is received.
choices.feedback: Receiving Announce does not make it grandmaster.

choices.text: It terminates PTP and regenerates all messages on a new VLAN.
choices.feedback: That describes neither transparent-clock forwarding nor correctionField behavior.

choices.text: It selects the best master through BMCA and disciplines its local clock.
choices.feedback: BMCA participation and local discipline describe a boundary clock.

questions.stem: Which messages measure adjacent-link delay in PTP peer-to-peer mode?

choices.text: Delay_Req and Delay_Resp exchanged only between slave and grandmaster.
choices.feedback: Delay_Req/Resp are the E2E path-delay mechanism.

choices.text: Announce and Sync messages exchanged only after a clock election.
choices.feedback: Announce/Sync establish hierarchy and time, not the P2P link-delay exchange.

choices.text: ARP Request and Reply messages exchanged between PTP VLAN peers.
choices.feedback: ARP does not measure PTP link delay.

choices.text: PDelay_Req, PDelay_Resp, and optional PDelay_Resp_Follow_Up.
choices.feedback: P2P measures each adjacent link with PDelay messages.

questions.stem: Which Layer-3 PTP transport does FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0 document?

choices.text: ipv4-UDP-mcast with transparent-p2p or boundary clock modes.
choices.feedback: The guide specifies IPv4 UDP multicast and the listed Layer-3 clock modes.

choices.text: l2-mcast with transparent-e2e and no Layer-3 address.
choices.feedback: L2 multicast is a Layer-2 transport, not the documented Layer-3 transport.

choices.text: ipv6-UDP-unicast with transparent-e2e on any RVI.
choices.feedback: The documented transport is IPv4 UDP multicast; transparent RVI mode is unsupported.

choices.text: tcp-ptp with boundary-e2e and no VLAN policy.
choices.feedback: PTP does not use the described TCP transport.

questions.stem: What is the documented P2P interaction with IGMP snooping?

choices.text: P2P requires IGMP snooping to be enabled on every VLAN.
choices.feedback: Enabling snooping does not make P2P interoperable.

choices.text: P2P uses IGMP snooping to elect the grandmaster clock.
choices.feedback: BMCA selects the master; IGMP does not.

choices.text: P2P mode is not interoperable with IGMP snooping.
choices.feedback: Fortinet explicitly documents P2P and IGMP snooping as incompatible.

choices.text: P2P requires static IGMP groups only when using IPv6 unicast.
choices.feedback: The static-group caveat applies to E2E IPv4 multicast with snooping.

questions.stem: Which AP and software combination is documented for Beacon Protection?

choices.text: Any Wi-Fi 5 FortiAP running FAP 7.2 or later.
choices.feedback: Wi-Fi 5 is not in the documented support scope.

choices.text: Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 FortiAP running FAP 7.6.1 or later.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents Wi-Fi 6E/7 hardware and FAP 7.6.1 or later.

choices.text: Any FortiAP running FortiOS 7.6.1 regardless of radio generation.
choices.feedback: The AP model and FortiAP software both matter.

choices.text: Only Wi-Fi 7 FortiAP running FAP 8.0.0 with WPA2 Enterprise.
choices.feedback: WPA2 is not the documented WPA3 Beacon Protection profile.

questions.stem: Which over-the-air evidence best confirms Beacon Protection is being advertised?

choices.text: The AP sends an EAP Access-Accept after the client association request.
choices.feedback: EAP success is authentication evidence, not beacon integrity evidence.

choices.text: The controller lists the SSID as enabled in the WTP profile.
choices.feedback: A WTP profile proves configuration, not the emitted beacon contents.

choices.text: The client receives an IPv4 address from the WLAN DHCP server.
choices.feedback: DHCP success occurs later and does not prove beacon protection.

choices.text: A beacon contains the Management MIC element and Beacon Protection capability flag.
choices.feedback: The Management MIC element and Extended Capabilities flag are the packet-level indicators.

questions.stem: Which VAP configuration dependency is required in Fortinet's Beacon Protection example?

choices.text: WPA2 security, PMF disabled, and rogue-AP detection enabled.
choices.feedback: This combination is inconsistent with the documented security requirements.

choices.text: Open authentication, captive portal, and a DHCP relay profile.
choices.feedback: Captive portal and DHCP relay do not enable beacon integrity.

choices.text: WPA3 security with PMF disabled and beacon protection left default.
choices.feedback: Beacon Protection is disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled.

choices.text: WPA3 security, PMF enabled, and beacon-protection enabled.
choices.feedback: The example uses WPA3 and enables PMF and Beacon Protection together.

questions.stem: What does Beacon Protection not provide by itself?

choices.text: Protection against RF jamming or complete rogue-AP prevention.
choices.feedback: Beacon integrity does not stop an attacker from transmitting or jamming RF energy.

choices.text: Integrity protection for supported beacon management frames.
choices.feedback: This is the intended feature behavior.

choices.text: A MIC element that a capable client can verify.
choices.feedback: This is part of the advertised protected-beacon information.

choices.text: A WPA3/PMF-related integrity mechanism on supported FortiAP radios.
choices.feedback: This describes the feature's supported scope.

questions.stem: Which FortiNAC notification method provides direct MAC Add/Delete/Move events from a FortiSwitch?

choices.text: SNMP Link Traps followed by an L2 poll of the port.
choices.feedback: Link traps trigger a poll; they do not carry the MAC move itself.

choices.text: A FortiGate interface status poll every five minutes.
choices.feedback: A periodic interface poll is not the documented MAC notification method.

choices.text: SNMP MAC Notification Traps from the switch.
choices.feedback: MAC Notification Traps carry the endpoint MAC event directly to FortiNAC.

choices.text: A RADIUS Access-Accept sent during the original 802.1X login.
choices.feedback: Access-Accept is authentication, not endpoint movement notification.

questions.stem: What is the key limitation of SNMP Link Traps for endpoint movement?

choices.text: They directly report every MAC address and exact downstream switch port.
choices.feedback: That describes direct MAC notifications, not link traps.

choices.text: They trigger L2 polling and may miss hosts behind indirect devices.
choices.feedback: A link event triggers a poll, which may not see endpoints behind phones, hubs, or APs.

choices.text: They are processed only when FortiClient EMS is licensed.
choices.feedback: EMS licensing is unrelated to SNMP link-trap processing.

choices.text: They carry full endpoint identity and user data in the trap.
choices.feedback: A link trap reports port state, not full endpoint identity.

questions.stem: What does FortiGate syslog MAC notification not process according to the guide?

choices.text: Access-point connection events are not processed through this syslog method.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly notes that AP connection events are not processed by this syslog method.

choices.text: MAC Add/Delete/Move events for FortiLink-managed FortiSwitches.
choices.feedback: These are the intended event types for FortiLink-managed switches.

choices.text: MAC movement events forwarded by the FortiGate to FortiNAC.
choices.feedback: This is the intended forwarding path.

choices.text: Syslog events received by FortiNAC from the configured FortiGate.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC can receive the configured syslog events.

questions.stem: FortiNAC shows no action behind a FortiLink-managed switch and FortiGate shows a blue icon. What should be checked first?

choices.text: The endpoint's OCSP responder and EAP-TLS certificate serial number.
choices.feedback: Certificate validation does not establish FortiLink device visibility.

choices.text: The FortiSwitch PTP domain and transparent-clock correction field.
choices.feedback: PTP is unrelated to NAC switch integration.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer EMS playbook schedule and OT vulnerability license.
choices.feedback: Asset enrichment is unrelated to the missing FortiSwitch model.

choices.text: FortiGate REST API integration, credentials, switch model, and interface synchronization.
choices.feedback: The recent scenario points to the integration/control plane before endpoint notification tuning.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates Access-Accept from CoA?

choices.text: Access-Accept changes an existing session; CoA performs initial authentication.
choices.feedback: The message roles are reversed.

choices.text: Access-Accept establishes initial access; CoA changes an existing session.
choices.feedback: CoA is a post-authentication change to an active RADIUS session.

choices.text: Both messages only disconnect the client and require a new DHCP lease.
choices.feedback: Neither message is defined only as a disconnect operation.

choices.text: CoA is an SNMP trap that updates the switch MAC table.
choices.feedback: CoA is a RADIUS dynamic-authorization message, not an SNMP trap.

questions.stem: What response is expected when a CoA requests a DACL on a port with DACL disabled?

choices.text: A CoA-ACK with the DACL silently ignored.
choices.feedback: The NAS does not acknowledge an unsupported DACL request as successful.

choices.text: An Access-Challenge requesting a new client certificate.
choices.feedback: Access-Challenge belongs to authentication, not this CoA response.

choices.text: A CoA-NAK indicating service not available.
choices.feedback: FortiSwitchOS returns a NAK with service not available when DACL is disabled.

choices.text: A Disconnect-ACK that confirms the policy was applied.
choices.feedback: A Disconnect-ACK is not the documented response for disabled DACL.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Filter-Id and NAS-Filter-Rule?

choices.text: Filter-Id carries rule text; NAS-Filter-Rule references a local ACL name.
choices.feedback: The attribute functions are reversed.

choices.text: Both attributes only identify the authenticated user's RADIUS group.
choices.feedback: These are ACL attributes, not only user-group identifiers.

choices.text: Both attributes are used only for IPv6 ACLs on wireless clients.
choices.feedback: FortiSwitch DACL support is IPv4, not IPv6.

choices.text: Filter-Id references a switch ACL; NAS-Filter-Rule carries rule text.
choices.feedback: Filter-Id names a preconfigured ACL, while NAS-Filter-Rule carries filter rules.

questions.stem: What can happen when a later CoA omits a DACL that was previously installed by CoA?

choices.text: The previously installed CoA DACL can be removed.
choices.feedback: FortiSwitchOS documents removal when the prior DACL was installed by CoA.

choices.text: The original Access-Accept is replayed and the port is rebooted.
choices.feedback: This is not the documented CoA behavior.

choices.text: The FortiNAC-F policy engine changes the switch's native VLAN.
choices.feedback: A CoA DACL update does not inherently change the native VLAN.

choices.text: The NAS automatically retains the last DACL until the session ends.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior is removal in this case, not guaranteed retention.

questions.stem: Which OCSP mode accepts a certificate when the responder times out, unless an explicit reject was received?

choices.text: Enable mode with strict OCSP verification on the profile.
choices.feedback: Strict Enable requires successful OCSP verification.

choices.text: Enable-softfail on the selected RADIUS authentication profile.
choices.feedback: Enable-softfail accepts on no response or timeout unless an explicit reject arrives.

choices.text: Disable mode, which still queries the responder but ignores results.
choices.feedback: Disable performs no OCSP verification; it does not query and ignore.

choices.text: CRL-only mode with no online certificate-status request.
choices.feedback: CRL checking is a separate revocation mechanism.

questions.stem: What is the documented OCSP timeout in FortiAuthenticator 8.0.2?

choices.text: One second, configurable per RADIUS client.
choices.feedback: The documented timeout is not one second or per-client.

choices.text: Five seconds, inherited from the EAP retransmission timer.
choices.feedback: EAP retransmission is a different timer.

choices.text: Three seconds, fixed in this release.
choices.feedback: The 8.0.2 release notes specify a fixed three-second timeout.

choices.text: Ten seconds, configurable on the OCSP responder object.
choices.feedback: The timeout is not documented as a ten-second responder setting.

questions.stem: Where is OCSP verification configured for EAP-TLS client certificates?

choices.text: In the RADIUS Auth Profile when Client Credential is Certificates.
choices.feedback: The option is per authentication profile under RADIUS Service and certificate client credentials.

choices.text: Globally under the FortiAuthenticator system DNS settings.
choices.feedback: DNS is a dependency for reaching a responder, not the policy control.

choices.text: On each FortiAP radio profile under the PMF option.
choices.feedback: The AP radio profile is not where FAC performs certificate OCSP validation.

choices.text: In the SCEP CA enrollment policy before a certificate is issued.
choices.feedback: SCEP issuance and runtime OCSP verification are separate stages.

questions.stem: What does a successful OCSP responder connection prove by itself?

choices.text: That the certificate subject maps to the intended user and group.
choices.feedback: User/group mapping is a separate authorization step.

choices.text: That the certificate is not revoked for every issuing CA.
choices.feedback: The response applies to a specific issuer and serial, not every CA.

choices.text: That the EAP-TLS handshake passed all authorization factors.
choices.feedback: OCSP is one check in the authentication flow, not the entire authorization result.

choices.text: Responder reachability, but not correct certificate-to-user authorization.
choices.feedback: Transport success proves reachability only; status and identity still need validation.

questions.stem: In FortiPAM SSH filtering, what is the practical difference between Allow and Deny mode?

choices.text: Allow blocks only matched commands; Deny blocks every unlisted command.
choices.feedback: The mode semantics are reversed.

choices.text: Allow blocks commands not matched; Deny blocks only matched commands.
choices.feedback: Allow is restricted mode; Deny blocks listed patterns while leaving other commands unblocked.

choices.text: Both modes allow unlisted commands and only log matched patterns.
choices.feedback: The modes do not both behave as audit-only filters.

choices.text: Both modes block all SSH commands unless owner bypass is enabled.
choices.feedback: Owner bypass is an exception, not the default state of every profile.

questions.stem: What does Bypass for owner permit when enabled?

choices.text: The secret owner can execute commands otherwise blocked by the SSH filter.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that the secret owner can send otherwise prohibited commands when bypass is enabled.

choices.text: Any delegated user can bypass all channel restrictions on the target.
choices.feedback: The bypass is specifically for the secret owner, not every delegated user.

choices.text: The SSH proxy stops recording commands for the secret owner.
choices.feedback: Command logging and channel controls are separate settings.

choices.text: The owner can bypass RADIUS authentication for the target server.
choices.feedback: This does not bypass target authentication.

questions.stem: Which control is required for FortiPAM Other Channels restrictions?

choices.text: A FortiGate NP7 link-scan profile assigned to the target subnet.
choices.feedback: NP7 link scanning is unrelated to SSH channel controls.

choices.text: A FortiAuthenticator OCSP profile attached to the secret owner.
choices.feedback: OCSP is a certificate status feature, not a channel restriction.

choices.text: A custom launcher for X11, forwarding, SFTP/SCP, and related channels.
choices.feedback: Fortinet notes that Other Channels settings require a custom launcher.

choices.text: A FortiSwitch PTP policy on the management VLAN.
choices.feedback: PTP does not control SSH forwarding channels.

questions.stem: What upgrade caveat applies to SSH filter profiles created on FortiPAM 1.3.0 or earlier?

choices.text: Legacy Deny entries become a default-deny profile automatically.
choices.feedback: The guide does not say legacy Deny entries become default deny.

choices.text: All legacy profiles are deleted and must be recreated manually.
choices.feedback: The profiles are not all deleted by the upgrade.

choices.text: Legacy patterns are converted into RADIUS Filter-Id attributes.
choices.feedback: RADIUS Filter-Id is unrelated to SSH filter profiles.

choices.text: Legacy Action=Allow entries may not block unlisted commands after upgrade.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that legacy Action=Allow entries are not shown in the new pattern table and do not block other commands.

questions.stem: Which Collector HA mechanism is used for on-premises and AWS deployments?

choices.text: A FortiGate SD-WAN rule with Lowest Cost SLA selection.
choices.feedback: SD-WAN is not the Collector HA mechanism.

choices.text: VRRP with a Leader, Followers, and a virtual IP.
choices.feedback: FortiSIEM documents VRRP for on-prem and AWS/EC2 Collector HA.

choices.text: An Active Directory site link with DNS round-robin records.
choices.feedback: AD site links and DNS do not implement the documented Collector VIP.

choices.text: A FortiAnalyzer log-forwarding policy with TCP acknowledgment.
choices.feedback: Log forwarding is a data transport feature, not Collector HA.

questions.stem: What happens when the FortiSIEM Collector Leader fails?

choices.text: A higher-priority Follower takes the VIP and jobs are redistributed.
choices.feedback: The new Leader owns the VIP, while Supervisor/App Server redistributes scheduled jobs.

choices.text: All Followers stop receiving logs until the Supervisor is restarted.
choices.feedback: Followers continue service through the HA mechanism.

choices.text: The Supervisor becomes the new Collector and owns the VIP.
choices.feedback: The Supervisor manages jobs but is not the Collector VIP owner.

choices.text: The failed Leader remains active while its interface is reachable.
choices.feedback: The failed node does not remain the active Leader after takeover.

questions.stem: Why might a stopped Collector process fail to trigger VRRP failover?

choices.text: VRRP requires a successful EAP-TLS certificate before changing roles.
choices.feedback: EAP-TLS is unrelated to Collector HA.

choices.text: The Supervisor prevents failover whenever syslog is enabled.
choices.feedback: Syslog does not disable VRRP role changes.

choices.text: VRRP may track interface state rather than the health of each process.
choices.feedback: Fortinet warns that process failure may not trigger VRRP when network state remains up.

choices.text: The VIP is moved only when the Collector database is corrupted.
choices.feedback: Database corruption is not the documented trigger.

questions.stem: What happens when a FortiSIEM Follower Collector goes down?

choices.text: The Leader immediately demotes itself and releases the VIP.
choices.feedback: Follower failure does not force the Leader to demote.

choices.text: The App Server redistributes its jobs to other working Collectors.
choices.feedback: The App Server redistributes jobs from a failed Follower; the returning node remains a Follower.

choices.text: The Supervisor deletes the failed Collector from the HA group permanently.
choices.feedback: The node can return as a Follower; permanent deletion is not automatic.

choices.text: All event-pulling jobs remain assigned until an administrator reboots the Leader.
choices.feedback: The guide describes automated job redistribution, not a mandatory reboot.

questions.stem: What is the direction of FortiManager central-management synchronization to FortiSASE?

choices.text: Bidirectional, with changes merged automatically in both systems.
choices.feedback: The documented workflow is not a bidirectional merge.

choices.text: One-way from FortiSASE to FortiManager after each policy install.
choices.feedback: The direction is reversed.

choices.text: Only identity objects synchronize; policies remain local to FortiSASE.
choices.feedback: Supported firewall and proxy policies are also synchronized.

choices.text: One-way from FortiManager to FortiSASE.
choices.feedback: The integration is a one-way source-of-truth workflow from FortiManager to FortiSASE.

questions.stem: Which FortiManager ADOM restriction applies when adding FortiSASE?

choices.text: Do not use FortiManager 7.0, Global Database ADOM, or Backup mode.
choices.feedback: FortiSASE cannot be added to a 7.0 ADOM, Global Database ADOM, or Backup-mode ADOM.

choices.text: Use only the Global Database ADOM with backup mode enabled.
choices.feedback: Those are explicitly excluded configurations.

choices.text: Add FortiSASE to any ADOM, then move it after installation.
choices.feedback: The device cannot be moved to another ADOM after it is added.

choices.text: Use a 7.0 ADOM and enable policy offload for synchronization.
choices.feedback: The 7.0 ADOM is unsupported and offload must be disabled.

questions.stem: FortiManager reports that a package installed successfully, but a FortiSASE policy is missing. What is the authoritative next check?

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiGate device database and clear all FortiAnalyzer logs.
choices.feedback: Those changes do not diagnose object-level synchronization.

choices.text: Change the FortiSASE WAN bandwidth policy and wait for the next SLA probe.
choices.feedback: Bandwidth policy and SLA probes are unrelated.

choices.text: Open FortiSASE Central Management Synchronization Log and inspect per-object errors.
choices.feedback: The FortiSASE synchronization log reports whether supported objects actually synchronized.

choices.text: Delete the FortiManager ADOM and recreate it in Global Database mode.
choices.feedback: Global Database ADOM is explicitly unsupported.

questions.stem: How should one-time schedule timestamps be handled during FortiManager synchronization?

choices.text: Enter local time and assume FortiSASE preserves the FortiManager timezone.
choices.feedback: The date/time picker is interpreted as GMT during synchronization.

choices.text: Use UTC epoch start-utc and end-utc values to avoid local-time ambiguity.
choices.feedback: The documented example treats the date/time picker as GMT and recommends UTC epoch fields.

choices.text: Convert every timestamp to the FortiSASE PoP's current local time.
choices.feedback: PoP local time is not the documented schedule conversion.

choices.text: Use the RADIUS accounting timestamp from the authentication server.
choices.feedback: RADIUS accounting timestamps are unrelated to schedule synchronization.

questions.stem: What does minimum-sla-meet-members control in a Lowest Cost (SLA) rule?

choices.text: The number of physical links that must be administratively up.
choices.feedback: Link-up alone is not the same as SLA qualification.

choices.text: The maximum number of sessions that can use each SD-WAN member.
choices.feedback: Session capacity is not what the option counts.

choices.text: The number of BGP neighbors that must advertise a community.
choices.feedback: BGP community advertisement is a separate routing mechanism.

choices.text: The minimum count of SLA-qualified members required for the rule to take effect.
choices.feedback: It is a rule-eligibility gate based on how many members meet the configured SLA.

questions.stem: If the minimum SLA member threshold is not met, what happens to the primary rule?

choices.text: All traffic is dropped immediately, regardless of later rules.
choices.feedback: A later rule or implicit rule may still forward traffic.

choices.text: The primary rule remains active and uses any alive member.
choices.feedback: The primary rule is not kept eligible when the threshold fails.

choices.text: It is skipped and evaluation continues to the next matching SD-WAN rule.
choices.feedback: The option gates rule eligibility; it does not inherently drop traffic.

choices.text: The FortiGate disables the Performance SLA health check globally.
choices.feedback: The health check remains configured; only the service rule is skipped.

questions.stem: Which member should count toward minimum-sla-meet-members?

choices.text: A member that is alive and satisfies the configured SLA thresholds.
choices.feedback: The threshold counts members that meet the SLA, not merely links that are up.

choices.text: Any member with carrier, even when latency and loss exceed limits.
choices.feedback: Carrier alone does not prove SLA compliance.

choices.text: A member that has a route but no successful health-check probe.
choices.feedback: A route without successful probes does not meet the configured SLA.

choices.text: A member selected by cost, even when its SLA map is failing.
choices.feedback: Cost ranking does not override the SLA pass condition.

questions.stem: Which diagnostics best show SLA qualification and rule selection for service 10?

choices.text: Only get system interface, because link state equals SLA state.
choices.feedback: Interface state does not expose all SLA metrics.

choices.text: Health-check status plus diagnose sys sdwan service4 10.
choices.feedback: The health-check diagnostic shows member SLA state; service4 shows service-rule selection.

choices.text: Only the routing table, because it records the selected SLA map.
choices.feedback: The routing table does not show the complete service SLA decision.

choices.text: Only a packet capture, because it shows the configured minimum threshold.
choices.feedback: A packet capture cannot show the configured rule threshold.
